To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the myelin protein Nogo‐A is a ligand for Caspr, an axonal component of paranodal junctions, and that Nogo‐ A and Caspr interact in trans at the paranode, where they may have a role modulating axon‐glial junction architecture.

Nogo‐66 is an oligodendrogial component congregating to and interacting with the axonal protein Caspr at CNS nodes of Ranvier, and that the interaction of Nogo‐66 with the Caspr protein may have a role during development and in pathological conditions.
Nogo‐66 binds to the paranodal complex, Caspr–Fas1/F3, and may have a role at the axon–glia junction during development and myelination.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of Nogo‐A in myelin formation, and in particular the role of Nog‐A at the paranode, a crucial site of myelin‐axon contact.
the identification and characterization of the molecular mechanisms that underlie the formation of axon–glia junctions and the role of Nogo‐A in this process.
the molecular basis of axon‐glial interaction at paranodes and its role in the regulation of K+‐channel organization and function during development.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
Nogo‐66 interacts in trans with the axonal Caspr–F-3 complex at CNS paranodes.
Nogo-A and Caspr interact at paranodes and that the Nogo-A-Caspr complex is important for paranodal structure formation.
Nogo‐66 is a ligand for Caspr and that the interaction of Nogo‐A with Caspr is a key event in the formation of axoglial junctions and the localization of Kv1 channels at the node of Ranvier.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Nogo‐66, a ligand of NgR, is also a ligand of the Caspr–Paranodin (Caspr) complex at paranodes, and this interaction may be involved in regulating paranodal K+ channel clustering during development.
paranodal Nogo–A–Caspr interaction may play a role in regulating K+‐channel distribution during myelination.
the interaction between Nogo and Caspr is important in regulating paranodal structure, and may have a role during development in regulating K+ channel localization.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Nogo‐66, the active component of Nogo‐A, interacts with Caspr, a major paranodal component.

Nogo‐66, the active component of the protein Nogo‐A (which is an inhibitor of axon growth in the central nervous system) is a ligand for Caspr, a protein that is part of the paranodal axoglial junction.
Nogo‐66 interacts in trans with Caspr at CNS axonal paranodes, an observation that may have implications for axon–glia junction architecture.
